acts.note.172:0.desc: Shortly after four o'clock on Friday afternoon, March 31, A.D. 30, Jesus and the apostles arrived at Bethany, and Jesus lodged with Simon, a neighboring believer. The chief priests decided not to seize him among his friends but to wait until he entered Jerusalem. That night the apostles, armed with swords, guarded him in pairs.
acts.note.172:1.desc: On the Sabbath evening six days before the Passover, the people of Bethany and Bethpage gave a banquet at Simon's house in honor of Jesus and Lazarus. Mary poured spikenard ointment on Jesus' head and feet; Judas called it waste, but Jesus defended her as preparing for his burial. Judas resolved to avenge this rebuke.
acts.note.172:1.diff: Matthew and Mark place it at the house of Simon the leper, where a woman anoints his head, whereas The Urantia Book has Mary anoint his head and feet at the home of the neighboring believer Simon. Unlike John, it does not call Judas a thief.
acts.note.172:2.desc: On Sunday morning in Simon's garden, Jesus gave the twelve final instructions before entering Jerusalem, telling them to do no public work during the Passover and to stay near him to watch and pray. He then advised Lazarus not to lose his life through the Sanhedrin's vengeance.
acts.note.172:3.desc: At half past one on Sunday afternoon, Jesus made his public entry into Jerusalem on a donkey's colt, in keeping with Zechariah's words. Peter and John brought the colt from Bethpage, and the crowds spread garments and branches, shouting hosanna. From the brow of Olivet Jesus wept over Jerusalem, and thousands came out of the city to meet him.
acts.note.172:3.diff: The Gospels say two unnamed disciples were sent, and Matthew mentions both a donkey and a colt, whereas The Urantia Book says Peter and John brought only the colt and that the welcoming crowd resulted from David Zebedee's spreading the news.
acts.note.172:4.desc: While the Alpheus twins returned the donkey, Jesus and the ten apostles strolled about the temple viewing the Passover preparations. Toward evening, by the treasury, Jesus saw a poor widow put in two mites and said she had given more than all the others, for she gave all her living. They then returned to Bethany to rest.
acts.note.172:4.diff: Mark and Luke place the widow's offering days later while Jesus taught in the temple, whereas The Urantia Book sets it on the evening of the Sunday entry, as they viewed the temple.
acts.note.172:5.desc: Returning to Bethany on Sunday evening, the apostles were silent. Peter and James were disappointed that Jesus had not proclaimed the kingdom; John and Matthew recalled Zechariah's prophecy; Nathaniel and Thomas saw the entry as a way to prevent his arrest. Judas, stung by a Sadducean friend's ridicule, was already a deserter at heart.
acts.map33.head: From Bethany to the Temple and the Gethsemane Camp
acts.map33.1.head: Monday, April 3 · Bethany to the temple
acts.map33.1.body: Early in the morning they assembled at the home of Simon, went down Mount Olivet, and arrived at the temple about nine o'clock; Jesus taught in the large court, and the temple was cleansed. About four o'clock they went back to Bethany (dashed), and he directed that a camp nearer the city be established.
acts.map33.2.head: Tuesday, April 4, morning · back to the temple court
acts.map33.2.body: About seven o'clock he said farewell at the home of Simon. Going toward Jerusalem with four apostles, he paused about halfway down the slope of Olivet for more than an hour, then taught in the temple court.
acts.map33.3.head: Noon · the home of Joseph
acts.map33.3.body: He received the Greeks and spoke at the luncheon; then he led the way over the narrow streets back to the temple and, shortly after two o'clock, began his last temple discourse.
acts.map33.4.head: Tuesday evening · to the camp near Gethsemane
acts.map33.4.body: Leaving the temple, they climbed a short distance up the western slope of Olivet; beholding the temple in the setting sun, Jesus spoke of its destruction, and they went on to the new camp a short distance above the public camping ground.
acts.map33.5.head: Wednesday, April 5 · a day in the hills
acts.map33.5.body: A day of rest. Jesus spent the whole day alone in the hills with John Mark and returned to the camp after sunset. The place in the hills is not given in the text.
acts.note.173:0.desc: Early Monday morning Jesus and the apostles met at Simon's home in Bethany and set out for Jerusalem. The apostles were silent because of his instruction to do no public teaching during Passover week, and Judas was pondering how to withdraw. About nine o'clock Jesus mounted a platform in the great temple court and began to teach.
acts.note.173:1.desc: The sale of sacrificial animals and money-changing in the temple courts brought huge profits to the high priest's family. On Monday morning Jesus took a scourge of cords from a lad and drove out the animals, the pilgrims overturned the money-changers' tables, and in five minutes the commerce was swept away. The court was quiet as Jesus taught all day.
acts.note.173:1.diff: The Gospel of John places the cleansing early in the ministry, whereas The Urantia Book puts it on Monday of the last week; and while the Gospels say Jesus overturned the tables, The Urantia Book says the pilgrims did.
acts.note.173:2.desc: At its noon meeting the Sanhedrin resolved to destroy Jesus and appointed five groups to entrap him. About two o'clock the elders of Israel asked by what authority he did these things. Jesus asked whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men, and when they said they did not know, he declined to answer.
acts.note.173:2.diff: The Gospels say chief priests, scribes, and elders asked, whereas The Urantia Book says it was the elders' group, one of five appointed by the Sanhedrin, and explains that Jesus did not rest his authority on John.
acts.note.173:3.desc: To the silent Pharisees Jesus told of two sons. One refused to work in the vineyard but later repented and went; the older son promised to go but did not. The first did the father's will, he said, and publicans and harlots would enter the kingdom ahead of them. The apostles took no part in these exchanges.
acts.note.173:3.diff: In Matthew the older son says he will go and does not, and the second repents and goes; The Urantia Book reverses the order, so the son first asked refuses then goes, and the older son fails to go.
acts.note.173:4.desc: Jesus told the crowd of a householder who let his vineyard to tenants and went to a far country. The tenants killed his servants and his steward, and at last his son. Citing the stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone, he warned that the kingdom would be taken from those who reject it. That night Sadducees and Pharisees joined forces.
acts.note.173:4.diff: The Gospels send the son right after the servants, whereas The Urantia Book adds the stage of sending and killing the steward, the most trusted servant. The saying that whoever falls on the stone, though broken, will be saved is not in the Bible.
acts.note.173:5.desc: Jesus told of a king whose invited guests refused his son's marriage feast and killed his messengers; the king destroyed them and called in all he found on the highways. A guest who would not wear the wedding garment freely provided was cast out. About four o'clock, returning to Bethany, Jesus directed that a camp be set up near Gethsemane.
acts.note.173:5.diff: The Gospel of Matthew binds the man without a garment and casts him into outer darkness, adding that few are chosen, whereas The Urantia Book says the king provided the garments free and the man was simply cast out.
acts.sub.173:5.4: "Destroy this temple, and in three days …"
acts.note.sub:173:5.4.desc: After the parable a sympathetic believer asked for a sign to know that Jesus was the Son of God. Pointing to his own body, Jesus said, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' Neither the people nor the apostles understood, and only after his resurrection did they recall the words.
acts.note.sub:173:5.4.diff: The Gospel of John places this early in the ministry after the temple cleansing, answering the Jews' demand for a sign, with a building time of forty-six years, whereas The Urantia Book has it answer a believer in the last week and says almost fifty years.
acts.note.174:0.desc: About seven o'clock on Tuesday morning Jesus met the apostles, the women's corps, and some two dozen disciples at Simon's home. He gave Lazarus the instruction that led him to flee to Philadelphia and gave his parting advice to the women's corps. After a personal word to each of the twelve, he set out for Jerusalem with Andrew, Peter, James, and John.
acts.note.174:1.desc: Going down Olivet, Peter asked who was right: James, who said the Father forgives before we ask, or himself, who held that repentance comes first. Jesus taught that God, like a wise parent, understands his children, so forgiveness is inevitable; sin is an experience of creature consciousness, and those who love their brothers have already forgiven them.
acts.note.174:2.desc: On Monday evening about fifty leaders agreed to discredit Jesus publicly. On Tuesday morning rehearsed young students, with Herodians, asked whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar. Jesus had them show a denarius bearing Caesar's image and answered, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's.'
acts.note.174:2.diff: Matthew says the Pharisees sent their disciples, whereas The Urantia Book says rehearsed young students came, and explains the answer by the Sanhedrin's rule that the right to coin money carried the right to levy taxes.
acts.note.174:3.desc: A group of Sadducees asked whose wife a woman married in turn to seven brothers would be in the resurrection. Jesus answered that the risen neither marry nor are given in marriage but are like the angels, and that the Father, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, is the God of the living. Some Pharisees cried out that he had answered well.
acts.note.174:3.diff: The Gospels give only the answer, whereas The Urantia Book explains that Jesus quoted only Moses to Sadducees who accepted only the books of Moses, and that he did not endorse the Pharisees' belief in a literal bodily resurrection.
acts.note.174:4.desc: A lawyer from the Pharisees asked which commandment was greatest. Jesus named loving God with all heart, soul, mind, and strength, and loving one's neighbor as oneself. He told the lawyer he was not far from the kingdom, and that night the lawyer was baptized. Toward noon Jesus asked how the Deliverer could be David's son.
acts.note.174:4.diff: Matthew says only that the lawyer asked to test him, whereas The Urantia Book says he was commended, professed faith that night at the camp, and was baptized by Josiah, and has Jesus speak of one commandment.
acts.note.174:5.desc: About noon on Tuesday, believing Greeks from Alexandria, Athens, and Rome asked Philip to see Jesus, and Philip and Andrew brought them to a luncheon at Joseph's house. Jesus spoke of the grain of wheat and prayed, 'Father, glorify your name,' and the personalized Adjuster appeared and answered.
acts.note.174:5.diff: The Gospel of John says a voice from heaven came and the crowd thought it thunder or an angel, whereas The Urantia Book says the personalized Adjuster spoke, those present did not hear the voice, and the setting was a luncheon at Joseph's house.
acts.note.175:0.desc: Shortly after two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, Jesus came to the temple with eleven apostles, Joseph of Arimathea, the thirty Greeks, and some disciples, and began his last address. The money-changers had not returned, so the court was quiet. This discourse was his last appeal to the Jewish people and the final indictment of their leaders.
acts.note.175:1.desc: In the temple courts Jesus offered a last chance of repentance to leaders who had rejected the Father's mercy, and told the people to follow the scribes' words but not their deeds. He pronounced woes on the hypocrites, lamented that he would have gathered them as a hen gathers her chicks, said their house was left desolate, and left the temple.
acts.note.175:1.diff: The Gospel of Matthew ends with their not seeing him until they bless him who comes in the Lord's name, whereas The Urantia Book has Jesus say he will teach no more in the temple and adds that he still offers mercy.
acts.note.175:2.desc: The rejection and plotting of Jesus' death by the Jewish leaders in no way affects any individual Jew's standing before God. Jesus himself was a Jew, and the first martyrs of the gospel were Jews; the revelators warn that persecution of Jews by professed Christians can never be justified.
acts.note.175:3.desc: At eight o'clock on Tuesday evening the Sanhedrin convened, and just before midnight on April 4, A.D. 30, it voted unanimously to impose the death sentence on both Jesus and Lazarus. This marked the rejection of the divine covenant. The officers were told to arrest Jesus secretly, not in public, and bring him in before midnight on Thursday.
acts.note.175:4.desc: Judas missed the first half of the discourse while conferring with Sadducean relatives about deserting, and the denunciation confirmed his decision to abandon the gospel. That night more than thirty secret believers met at Nicodemus's home and agreed to acknowledge the Master openly the hour he was arrested. The Sanhedrin set its next meeting at Caiaphas's home.
acts.intro.176: The destruction of the temple foretold
acts.note.176:0.desc: As they left the temple on Tuesday afternoon, Matthew pointed out its massive stones and adornment, and Jesus said not one stone would be left upon another. The group climbed Olivet and sat watching the temple glow in the sunset and under the full moon, and Nathaniel asked how they would know when these things would happen.
acts.note.176:0.diff: The Gospels say the disciples, one of them, or some people pointed to the buildings, whereas The Urantia Book names Matthew and says it was Nathaniel who asked about the time.
acts.note.176:1.desc: On Olivet Jesus told them not to fear false deliverers, wars, or persecution, and to flee to the hills when Roman armies surrounded Jerusalem. Heeding this warning, believers fled to Pella when the Roman armies first appeared. When Peter asked about his return, Jesus rebuked him for trying to attach the new teaching to the old.
acts.note.176:1.diff: The Gospels tie these words to signs of the world's end, the second coming, and the abomination of desolation, whereas The Urantia Book treats them as practical instructions to flee Jerusalem's destruction and adds that believers escaped to Pella.
acts.note.176:2.desc: Jesus set aside the expectation that the Son of Man would sit on David's throne, promising to be with them through the Spirit of Truth and to return to this world someday. The time is known only in the councils of Paradise, and each person meets judgment and a new dispensation individually upon passing through the portals of death.
acts.note.176:2.diff: The Gospels speak of a darkened sun and moon and the Son of Man coming on the clouds, whereas The Urantia Book says a Jewish apocalyptic by one Selta was copied into Matthew here, and speaks only of a return in power and spirit.
acts.note.176:3.desc: At the campfire Thomas asked how they should conduct themselves while the Master was away. Jesus said that their relation to the kingdom is spiritual and personal, so the downfall of nations and the end of an age cannot shake a believer. Each generation should work with his return in mind, as with death, and living faith must bear the fruits of the spirit.
acts.note.176:3.diff: The Gospels place this parable within the Olivet discourse, whereas The Urantia Book has Jesus speak it that night by the campfire near Gethsemane to some twenty people in answer to Thomas's question.
acts.note.sub:176:3.4–9.desc: A man leaving for a far country entrusted his servants with five, two, and one talents according to their abilities. Two doubled their talents, but the one who received one talent hid it in the ground and lost even that. Jesus and the revelators explain that merely preserving truth in fixed forms is also unfruitful stewardship.
acts.note.sub:176:3.4–9.diff: The Gospel of Matthew ends by casting the worthless servant into outer darkness with weeping and gnashing of teeth, whereas The Urantia Book stops with taking away his talent and adds that merely preserving truth is also slothfulness.
acts.note.176:4.desc: Along with promising the Spirit of Truth, Jesus promised to return in person to this world someday, but did not say how, where, or when. The revelators think Michael may return more than once but do not know the time, and urge believers not to tie his return to particular events but to be always ready.
acts.note.177:0.desc: On Wednesday morning Jesus told the apostles to rest and meditate, and told Andrew he would be away for the day and that none should go within Jerusalem's gates. He declined David Zebedee's offer of three armed guards, saying he wished to commune alone with the Father, and John Mark came forward with a lunch basket.
acts.note.177:1.desc: When John Mark held on to the basket and asked to go along, Jesus took him into the hills, where they spent the Master's last tranquil day on earth until after sundown. Jesus assured the youth that he would survive to become a mighty messenger of the kingdom and charged him to tell no one what he had heard.
acts.note.177:2.desc: Comparing boyhoods with John Mark, Jesus said John would prove loyal because loving and wise parents had reared him, unlike his friend Amos, whose overfond parents had not let him come. Because a child forms his concept of the heavenly Father from his earthly father, early home life shapes the whole of life.
acts.note.177:3.desc: The apostles spent the day visiting disciples on Olivet while waiting for Jesus, and Nathaniel spoke on supreme desire. David Zebedee received word that Jesus' family was coming to Jerusalem but kept it secret. More than twenty Greeks came to the camp and conferred with Peter and John, and the leaders were surprised that Jesus did not appear.
acts.note.177:4.desc: On Wednesday, ignoring the Master's request, Judas went to an informal Sanhedrin meeting at Caiaphas's home, introduced by his cousin, and asked what they would give him to deliver Jesus quietly. Caiaphas promised a reward after the delivery, and Judas agreed with the captain of the guards on an arrest Thursday night. His motive was not money but self-glory and revenge.
acts.note.177:4.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says they weighed out thirty pieces of silver and Luke says Satan entered Judas, whereas The Urantia Book defers the reward until after the betrayal and attributes his motive to self-glory and accumulated resentment rather than money.
acts.note.177:5.desc: At Wednesday evening's social hour at the camp, Jesus tried to cheer the downcast apostles, asked about their families, and warned them not to rely on the support of superficially believing crowds but to watch and pray. Word spread that Lazarus had fled from Bethany, and this was the apostles' lowest spiritual point before Jesus' death.
acts.map34.head: The Gethsemane Camp and the Upper Chamber
acts.map34.1.head: Morning · the farewell address
acts.map34.1.body: Soon after breakfast he led them to a secluded spot a short distance above the camp and gave his farewell address to the apostles and chosen disciples; at almost one o'clock they went back to the camp.
acts.map34.2.head: Half past four · to the upper chamber
acts.map34.2.body: Over the western brow of Mount Olivet to the road from Bethany; they paused where he had tarried the previous evening, waited until sunset, went down into the city, and ate the Last Supper in the upper chamber of the Mark home. Streets in the city are approximate.
acts.map34.3.head: About ten o'clock · back to the camp
acts.map34.3.body: He led the eleven apostles through the city, over the brook Kidron, and on to their encampment adjacent to Gethsemane Park. Judas was already gone.
acts.map34.4.head: Prayer in the near-by ravine
acts.map34.4.body: When the camp was still, he took Peter, James, and John a short way up a near-by ravine where he had often gone to pray.
acts.map34.5.head: The olive press
acts.map34.5.body: Leaving his followers, he walked down to the olive press near the entrance to Gethsemane Park and sat there alone, awaiting the betrayer (the arrest is on Map 35).
acts.note.178:0.desc: After breakfast on Thursday, Jesus led the apostles and the Jewish and gentile disciples to a secluded spot above the camp and gave his farewell address to the whole camp group. Judas was absent; some thought he had been sent to the city to prepare for the Passover, and he returned to the camp only in midafternoon.
acts.note.178:1.desc: On Thursday forenoon Jesus taught about fifty trusted followers for almost two hours on the relation of the kingdom of heaven to the kingdoms of this world and of sonship to citizenship. Believers should render to Caesar and to God their due, never spread truth by secular power, and as better citizens carry the gospel as a living seed.
acts.note.178:2.desc: By noon all knew of Lazarus's flight. When David Zebedee asked whether Jesus knew of Judas's plot, Jesus said he knew all and told him to say nothing. He sent Peter, John, and Philip to follow a man carrying a water pitcher to the upper room of John Mark's home, and Judas turned all the apostolic funds over to David.
acts.note.178:2.diff: The Gospels say the disciples were sent to prepare the Passover, whereas The Urantia Book says it was a supper the night before the Passover, arranged by Jesus with John Mark the previous day, and identifies the place as John Mark's home.
acts.note.178:3.desc: Near sundown on Thursday, Jesus and the twelve crossed the western brow of Mount Olivet toward the city and paused where he had spoken the evening before. He said that as the Father had sent him, so he would send them, and warned them not to endanger themselves defending the Son of Man. After sunset they went on to the home of John Mark.
acts.note.179:0.desc: When Philip asked about the Passover, he meant the supper due on Friday evening, but Jesus held his supper a day early, on Thursday evening, and the apostles did not understand why. Since Jesus had never provided a lamb when acting as host, they were not surprised that none was served. John Mark's parents welcomed them, and they went up to the upper chamber.
acts.note.179:1.desc: Inside the door of the upper chamber stood pitchers of water and basins for washing feet, but no servant, and none of the apostles would act as servant. Judas took the place of honor at the host's left and John the right, so Peter angrily took the lowest seat. Jesus entered amid the quarrel and silently took his place, looking disappointed.
acts.note.179:2.desc: Seated, Jesus smiled and said he had greatly desired to eat this Passover with them before he suffered. He took the cup from Thaddeus, gave thanks, and had them share it, saying he would not drink with them again until they sat together in the coming kingdom. He knew Judas's intent but was concerned only for his followers' safety.
acts.note.179:2.diff: The Gospel of Luke portrays this meal as the Passover, whereas The Urantia Book makes it a supper without a lamb on Thursday evening, a day before the Passover, and says Thaddeus handed Jesus the cup.
acts.note.179:3.desc: After the first cup, Jesus laid aside his outer garment, girded himself with a towel, and knelt before Peter in the lowest seat. Peter first refused, then asked him to wash his hands and head too. Jesus washed the feet of all twelve, Judas included, rebuked their struggle for places, and taught that whoever would be first must be as one who serves.
acts.note.179:3.diff: The Gospel of John sets it during supper and says the devil had put the idea into Judas's heart, whereas The Urantia Book places it after the first cup as an acted parable for apostles who refused to wash one another's feet and quarreled over seats.
acts.note.179:4.desc: In the middle of the second course, Jesus explained why he was eating this supper a day early and said that his going to the Father was necessary, but not that one of them become a traitor. When Judas asked, 'Is it I?' Jesus gave him the dipped bread and said, 'You have said.' Told to act quickly, Judas went out into the night.
acts.note.179:4.diff: The Gospels say the Son of Man goes as it is written and John says Satan entered Judas after the morsel, whereas The Urantia Book says the betrayal was not needed for the Father's will but was the fruit of evil hidden in Judas's heart.
acts.note.179:5.desc: Jesus took the third cup, the cup of blessing, and called it the cup of blessing of a new dispensation and the emblem of the bestowal of the Spirit of Truth. He then broke the bread, calling it the bread of life. He instituted the remembrance supper with symbols so as to avoid binding forms, and they closed by singing the 118th Psalm.
acts.note.179:5.diff: The Gospels give the bread first as his body and the cup as covenant blood shed for the remission of sins, whereas The Urantia Book has the cup first, as the emblem of the Spirit of Truth, and calls the bread the bread of life.
acts.intro.180: The beginning of the farewell discourse
acts.note.180:0.desc: After the supper and the psalm, Jesus had the apostles sit down again and told them they could no longer go out without purse as before but must now provide for themselves. The hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified; he was going where they could not yet go, but when their work was done they would come to him.
acts.note.180:0.diff: The Gospel of Luke says whoever has no sword should sell his cloak and buy one, whereas The Urantia Book has nothing about a sword and says only that he who has a purse should take it with him.
acts.note.180:1.desc: Going beyond the commandment to love one's neighbor as oneself, Jesus gave the new commandment to love one another as he had loved them. No greater love exists than to lay down one's life for one's friends, and he called the apostles friends, not servants. The revelators add that Jesus asks not for sacrifice but for loyalty.
acts.note.180:1.diff: John chapter 13 gives only the brief new commandment, whereas The Urantia Book continues here with the greater love of laying down one's life for friends and the calling of friends rather than servants, which the Bible places in chapter 15.
acts.note.180:2.desc: Jesus teaches that he is the true vine, the Father the husbandman, and the apostles the branches; abiding in him, they bear much fruit of loving service. The revelators point out the later misunderstanding that treated prayer in Jesus' name as magic, and explain prayer as the experience of recognizing and doing the Father's will.
acts.note.180:2.diff: The Gospel of John says to ask whatever you will and it shall be done, whereas The Urantia Book says to ask what the spirit desires, notes that this saying was misrecorded and misunderstood, and omits burning the branches.
acts.note.180:3.desc: Jesus told them not to be discouraged by the world's hatred and persecution, since it hated him first, and promised to send a spirit helper after he left. In the Father's universe are many abodes, and he would receive them there. To Thomas he said, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life,' and to Philip that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.
acts.note.180:3.diff: John chapter 15 speaks of the world's hatred and the Comforter's witness, whereas The Urantia Book joins here the many abodes and the answers to Thomas and Philip, which the Bible places in chapter 14, explaining the abodes as the Father's worlds of light.
acts.note.180:4.desc: Jesus said that after going to the Father and receiving final sovereignty, he would pour out the Spirit of Truth upon all flesh, leaving in the flesh so as to be with them more fully in spirit. When Judas Alpheus asked how they would know him if he came only in spirit, Jesus answered that the Spirit of Truth would live in each one's heart.
acts.note.180:4.diff: The Gospel of John says the Father gives the Comforter, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus sends the Spirit of Truth with the Father's approval, and that this spirit is his own, like him except for the material body.
acts.note.180:5.desc: The revelators explain that the promised helper, the Spirit of Truth, is not the letter or law of truth but the living conviction of true meanings on real spirit levels. Truth cannot be confined in formulas or creeds, and even the golden rule and nonresistance are rightly understood only through the living interpretation of the Spirit of Truth.
acts.note.180:5.diff: The Gospel of John says the Comforter will convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment, whereas The Urantia Book lacks this saying and explains the Spirit of Truth as the growing conviction of truth within the believer.
acts.note.180:6.desc: Jesus warned that a time would come when those who kill them would think they served God, and said he must leave so the Spirit of Truth could come and guide them into all truth. He explained his saying about leaving for a little while and being seen again by the figure of a woman in travail, but the eleven, bound by messianic ideas, did not understand.
acts.note.180:6.diff: The Gospel of John says only that their sorrow will turn to joy when they see him again, whereas The Urantia Book says they will not see him long even then, since he goes to the Father, and plainly foretells his death and resurrection.
acts.note.181:0.desc: After the farewell discourse Jesus visited informally with the eleven, recounting many experiences, and they slowly realized that he was about to leave them. Many took his promise to return after a little while to mean he would soon come back to set up the kingdom. Then Jesus called them to order again and began his final admonitions.
acts.note.181:1.desc: Jesus told the eleven that once delivered from the flesh he would return as a spirit indweller of every believer, and he spoke of ceaseless progression through the many stations in the Father's house. He left them his peace, unlike the world's, and comforted them: even when they scattered and left him alone, the Father was with him, for he had overcome the world.
acts.note.181:1.diff: The Gospel of John records the disciples saying he now speaks plainly and they believe, and Jesus asking whether they now believe; The Urantia Book omits this exchange and instead explains the peace of Jesus.
acts.note.181:2.desc: Jesus went around the table giving each apostle personal counsel and a blessing. He entrusted his earthly family to John, released Andrew from administrative responsibility, and spoke to Simon Zelotes, Matthew, James, the twins, Philip, Nathaniel, Thomas, and Peter about their weaknesses and missions. After singing a hymn, they departed for the camp on the Mount of Olives.
acts.note.181:2.diff: The Bible has no individual farewell admonitions to each apostle in the upper room; The Urantia Book places here the entrusting of Jesus' family to John and Andrew's release from leadership.
acts.note.sub:181:2.27–30.desc: Jesus pointed out Peter's weakness of speaking before thinking and warned that all were in danger of stumbling that night, but promised that after his return he would go before them into Galilee. When Peter vowed to die for him, Jesus said Peter would deny him three or four times before the cock crowed.
acts.note.sub:181:2.27–30.diff: Matthew and Mark place the prediction of three denials after the hymn, on the way to the Mount of Olives, whereas The Urantia Book has Jesus foretell three or four denials in the upper chamber.
acts.note.182:0.desc: About ten o'clock on Thursday night Jesus led the eleven from the home of Elijah and Mary Mark back to the Gethsemane camp, followed by John Mark in his linen coat. For the first time the apostles suspected Judas, and when he was not at the camp either, Andrew said he feared Judas had deserted them.
acts.note.182:1.desc: Soon after reaching camp, Jesus had the eleven kneel in a circle about him on a large flat rock on Olivet and, standing in the moonlight, prayed that the Father would glorify the Son and that the apostles, and all who would believe through them, might be one. The narrator explains that Jesus revealed the Father's name through his life.
acts.note.182:1.diff: The Gospel of John places this prayer at the end of the supper discourse and calls Judas the son of perdition, whereas The Urantia Book sets it on a rock above the camp with the apostles kneeling and calls Judas the son of revenge.
acts.note.182:2.desc: David Zebedee and John Mark told Jesus they had been watching Judas. Simon Zelotes handed out swords, and nine apostles armed themselves, all except Nathaniel and Andrew. Jesus sent the messenger Jacob to Abner at Philadelphia, charged the chief of the Greeks and Andrew, and David told him his family was in Jericho.
acts.note.182:3.desc: Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a nearby ravine and, about a stone's throw away, prayed three times; each time he found the three apostles asleep. A mighty angel came down to strengthen him and convey the Father's will. After great agony Jesus regained his poise and prepared to meet the betrayer.
acts.note.182:3.diff: Luke says his sweat was like drops of blood, whereas The Urantia Book says it ran in great drops; his first prayer was not to remove the cup but to know that drinking it was the Father's will.
acts.note.183:0.desc: Jesus urged the three apostles to go to their tents and sleep, but when messengers came seeking David, a Greek sentinel roused his countrymen, and the whole camp except the eight apostles awoke. To keep his followers from being arrested with him, Jesus withdrew and sat alone on the olive press near the entrance to Gethsemane Park, awaiting the betrayer.
acts.note.183:1.desc: The narrator explains that the cruel treatment and unfair trial of Jesus were not part of the Father's will. The Father desired the bestowal Son to finish his earth career naturally, as all mortals must; Jesus refused to save himself from the march of events, and the cruelty was the work of evil men.
acts.map35.head: From the Arrest in Gethsemane to the Trial before Pilate
acts.map35.sub: Night of April 6 – morning of April 7, A.D. 30  ·  Papers 183–185
acts.map35.1.head: The arrest · to the palace of Annas
acts.map35.1.body: About half after eleven o'clock Judas started out from the temple with temple guards and Roman soldiers. Jesus, sitting alone on the olive press, was arrested and, by order of the Roman captain, taken to the palace of Annas, the former high priest, on Mount Olivet.
acts.map35.2.head: The palace of Caiaphas · the Sanhedrist court
acts.map35.2.body: Nearing the break of day, Annas sent Jesus bound to Caiaphas. About half past three the Sanhedrist court was called to order; at five-thirty it reassembled to formulate the charges for Pilate.
acts.map35.3.head: Before Pilate
acts.map35.3.body: At six o'clock he was led forth from the home of Caiaphas and tried before Pilate in front of the praetorium, an addition to the fortress of Antonia.
acts.map35.4.head: Before Herod
acts.map35.4.body: He was taken to the old Maccabean palace of Herod the Great, where Herod Antipas dwelt when in Jerusalem.
acts.map35.5.head: Back to Pilate
acts.map35.5.body: The guards brought Jesus back to Pilate; about half past eight the hearing ended, and he was placed in the custody of the Roman soldiers (Map 36).
acts.note.183:2.desc: Leaving the supper, Judas went with his cousin to the captain of the temple guards and led him to the Mark home, but Jesus had gone. Fearing the armed disciples, Judas asked for forty armed soldiers, and the Jewish authorities obtained Pilate's permission to use Roman guards. About half past eleven more than sixty persons set out from the temple.
acts.note.183:3.desc: When the band arrived with torches, Jesus asked from the olive press whom they sought and declared, "I am he," and the front ranks fell backward. Judas kissed him on the forehead anyway, and Jesus asked whether he would betray him with a kiss. When Malchus moved to bind him, Peter drew his sword, but Jesus stopped him; John Mark fled naked, leaving his linen coat.
acts.note.183:3.diff: The Bible says the high priest's servant lost his ear to the sword, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus stopped Peter before any blow; it adds that Judas kissed Jesus though Jesus had already identified himself.
acts.note.183:4.desc: After the arrest the apostles gathered at the olive press. Simon Zelotes urged a rescue, but Nathaniel and James recalled the teaching of nonresistance, and at Thomas's urging they all scattered. David Zebedee stayed at the camp to run the messenger headquarters, and at daybreak Jude, Jesus' brother, arrived bringing word for the family.
acts.note.183:5.desc: Before leaving the garden, the captain of the temple guards wanted to take Jesus to Caiaphas, but under orders the Roman captain led him to the palace of Annas. The Roman officer protected John Zebedee, who had not drawn a sword, letting him stay near the Master, while shamed Judas fell behind. Jesus spoke no word until he stood before Annas.
acts.note.184:0.desc: As Annas had arranged, the Roman captain brought the arrested Jesus to the palace of Annas on Mount Olivet. Annas wanted to gain time, since the Sanhedrin could not lawfully convene before the morning sacrifice in the temple; meanwhile some thirty members of the Sanhedrin gathered at the palace of Caiaphas.
acts.note.184:1.desc: Annas hoped to send Jesus out of Palestine but faltered before his dignity and questioned him about his disciples and teachings. When Jesus told him to ask those who had heard him, the chief steward struck him in the face. Asked whether he was the Messiah, Jesus answered only that Annas had said it.
acts.note.184:1.diff: The Gospel of John briefly reports the high priest's questions and an officer's blow; The Urantia Book adds Annas's plan to send Jesus out of the country, the exchange about the Messiah, and about three hours of detention.
acts.note.184:2.desc: John asked the portress to let Peter into the courtyard of Annas's palace. By the fire and on the porch, Peter repeatedly denied being Jesus' disciple when the portress and servants challenged him, and at the cock's crow he remembered the Master's warning. When Jesus, being led to Caiaphas, looked at him, Peter sat by the roadside and wept bitterly.
acts.note.184:2.diff: The Synoptic Gospels place the three denials in the high priest's courtyard, whereas The Urantia Book says everything occurred at Annas's palace on Mount Olivet, the cock's crow showing it was outside Jerusalem.
acts.note.184:3.desc: About half past three on Friday morning, Caiaphas called to order a court of some thirty Sanhedrists at his palace. The false witnesses contradicted one another while Jesus stood silent. When asked whether he was the Son of God, Jesus said, "I am"; Caiaphas rent his garments, and the members declared him worthy of death, spitting on him and striking him.
acts.note.184:3.diff: The Bible says the whole council assembled, whereas The Urantia Book says only about thirty hostile Sanhedrists met at the high priest's palace; Jesus' answer speaks of soon going to the Father rather than coming on the clouds.
acts.note.184:4.desc: During the hour the court recessed, the temple guards and the high priest's servants mocked Jesus, spat on him, struck him with sticks, and told him to prophesy who had hit him. Jesus had John withdraw to an adjoining room and uttered no word. The Urantia Book calls this hour of humiliation among the Master's greatest victories.
acts.note.184:4.diff: The Bible briefly reports the abuse; The Urantia Book adds that Jesus sent John away and interprets this hour as a victory revealing man to God.
acts.note.184:5.desc: Reassembling at five-thirty, the court drew up within half an hour three charges: perverting the nation, teaching refusal of tribute to Caesar, and inciting treason by claiming to be a king. Agreed upon without witnesses and in the prisoner's absence, the charges led three Pharisees to leave. At six o'clock Jesus was led to Pilate.
acts.note.184:5.diff: Luke says the council summoned Jesus at daybreak and asked whether he was the Christ, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus did not appear at the second session, and a similar answer was given to a woman who came to look at him.
acts.note.185:0.desc: Shortly after six o'clock on Friday morning, April 7, A.D. 30, Jesus was brought bound before the Roman procurator Pilate, with some fifty accusers. The public trial was held outside on the steps of the praetorium, beside the fortress of Antonia, because the Jews would not enter a gentile building and be defiled on the preparation day.
acts.note.185:1.desc: Pontius Pilate governed Judea for ten years as a reasonably capable administrator but was a moral coward. He clashed with the Jews over Caesar's images on military standards, the emperor's shields in Herod's palace, and using temple funds for an aqueduct, and he yielded each time. Later recalled over a massacre of Samaritans, he retired to Lausanne and took his own life.
acts.note.185:2.desc: When Pilate asked for the accusation, the Sanhedrists demanded only that he confirm the death sentence. When Pilate refused to proceed without written charges, three were submitted: perverting the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and calling himself the king of the Jews. Jesus made no reply.
acts.note.185:2.diff: The Synoptic Gospels have Pilate ask at once whether he is the king of the Jews, whereas The Urantia Book says he first demanded written charges and asked that question later in a private examination.
acts.note.185:3.desc: Pilate took Jesus and John into a private chamber and verified the tribute question with John. Asked whether he was the king of the Jews, Jesus answered that his kingdom was not of this world but spiritual, and that he came to bear witness to the truth. Convinced of his innocence, Pilate learned he was a Galilean and sent him to Herod.
acts.note.185:3.diff: The Gospel of John has no testimony by John on the tribute question; The Urantia Book also reports Jesus describing his kingdom more fully as the family of the faith sons, open even to gentiles.
acts.note.185:4.desc: Herod Antipas questioned Jesus for some fifteen minutes in the old Maccabean palace and urged him to work a wonder, but Jesus did not answer. Herod did not recognize him as the lad who once petitioned him at Sepphoris about his father's compensation. After making fun of him, Herod arrayed him in an old purple royal robe and sent him back to Pilate.
acts.note.185:4.diff: Luke says Herod and Pilate became friends that day, which The Urantia Book does not mention; instead it adds that Herod failed to recognize the boy from Sepphoris and still feared over John the Baptist.
acts.note.185:5.desc: Pilate said Jesus was innocent and offered to chastise and release him, but when a crowd arrived seeking the Passover pardon, he asked whether they wanted Barabbas or Jesus. The chief priests cried for Barabbas, and the crowd joined in. While a letter from his wife Claudia delayed the verdict, the crowd shouted again and again, "Crucify him!"
acts.note.185:5.diff: The Bible presents Barabbas only as an insurrectionist and murderer, whereas The Urantia Book calls him a priest's son taken on the Jericho road; Claudia's note delayed the verdict, giving the rulers time to stir up the crowd.
acts.note.185:6.desc: To win the crowd's pity, Pilate had Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mocked him with a purple robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed. Pilate declared, "Behold the man!" but the crowd shouted all the louder. When the high priest said Jesus made himself out to be the Son of God, Pilate grew more afraid.
acts.note.185:6.diff: Matthew and Mark place the mocking after the death sentence, whereas The Urantia Book, like John, says Pilate had Jesus flogged before sentencing to gain pity and stopped it partway.
acts.note.185:7.desc: Pilate again sat alone with Jesus and asked where he came from and who he really was. Jesus answered that Pilate would have no power unless it were allowed from above, and that those who delivered him had the greater sin. When Pilate moved to release him, Caiaphas threatened that he was no friend of Caesar, and the crowd cried that they had no king but Caesar.
acts.note.185:7.diff: The Gospel of John says the Jews cried out together, whereas The Urantia Book says the high priest Caiaphas himself shook a finger in Pilate's face, threatening to report him to the emperor.
acts.note.185:8.desc: Fearing a riot and Caesar's reprimand, Pilate released Barabbas. He washed his hands in a basin of water before the crowd, saying he was innocent of this man's blood, and handed Jesus over to the soldiers. The crowd shouted that his blood be on them and their children.
acts.note.186:0.desc: On the way to Herod, Jesus told John to bring his mother, and John went to Jesus' family at the home of Martha and Mary in Bethany. Mary set out with John, followed by Jesus' sister Ruth and brother Jude, but by the time they reached the city, Jesus was already at Golgotha.
acts.note.186:1.desc: On Friday morning Judas sought his reward from the Sanhedrin, but a servant gave him only thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave. Seeing the cross raised, he tried to return the money, saying he had betrayed innocent blood; mocked, he threw the silver over the temple floor. He hanged himself from a cliff in the valley of Hinnom.
acts.note.186:1.diff: Matthew says the silver bought the potter's field, which The Urantia Book omits; it says the money was a reward paid by a servant after Jesus was delivered, and that the knot gave way and Judas fell on the rocks.
acts.note.186:2.desc: Jesus showed no interest in the details of his trials but always answered the one question about his mission, whether he was the Son of God. He was silent before Herod and spoke to Pilate only to enlighten him. When Pilate said, "Behold the man!" all Nebadon heard the cry to behold God and man.
acts.note.186:3.desc: David Zebedee moved his tent up the ravine to serve as messenger headquarters, and the temple guards burned the deserted camp. He sent runners far and wide and dispatched reports about every half hour. Taking literally the promise to rise on the third day, he planned to assemble his messengers early Sunday morning at the home of Nicodemus.
acts.map36.head: From the Praetorium to Golgotha
acts.map36.1.head: Delivered up at the praetorium
acts.map36.1.body: The praetorium, an addition to the fortress of Antonia. Pilate washed his hands before the multitude and turned Jesus over to the Roman soldiers, who led him back into the courtyard of the praetorium and dressed him in his own garments. It was a little after eight o'clock.
acts.map36.2.head: The way to Golgotha
acts.map36.2.body: Just before nine o'clock they started out by the most direct route to the Damascus gate, which led out of the city to the north. On the way Simon from Cyrene carried the crossbeam; shortly after nine o'clock they arrived at Golgotha.
acts.map36.3.head: Golgotha · the cross
acts.map36.3.body: At about half past nine he was hung upon the cross between two brigands; just before three o'clock he gave up the life struggle.
acts.map36.4.head: Laid in Joseph's new tomb
acts.map36.4.body: At about half past four the burial procession went from Golgotha to Joseph's new tomb, hewn out of solid rock, a short distance north of Golgotha and across the road leading to Samaria.
acts.note.186:4.desc: Pilate turned Jesus over to the Roman soldiers with orders to crucify him at once. The soldiers removed the robe Herod had put on him and dressed him in his own clothes, and the captain's decision to take along two condemned thieves delayed the start until a little before nine. All this while Jesus said nothing.
acts.note.186:4.diff: The Bible says only that they led him out after the mocking, whereas The Urantia Book says the robe removed was Herod's and that the departure was delayed to take two thieves along.
acts.note.186:5.desc: Jesus died near the hour of the Passover sacrifice, but his death has no relation to the Jewish sacrificial system; men, not God, planned it. He did not die as a sacrifice for sin or to atone for mankind's guilt. Sonship with God depends not on his death but on spirit-born faith.
acts.note.187:0.desc: The captain who had arrested Jesus in Gethsemane led twelve soldiers taking Jesus and two thieves to the place of crucifixion. The thieves were associates of Barabbas, so Jesus in effect was crucified in Barabbas's place. Just before nine in the morning the procession left the praetorium, followed by more than two hundred people.
acts.note.187:1.desc: Jesus carried the crossbeam to Golgotha behind the board Pilate had inscribed in three languages, "Jesus of Nazareth—the King of the Jews." He told the weeping women to weep for themselves and their children. After passing through the city gate he fell, and the captain compelled Simon of Cyrene to carry the crossbeam.
acts.note.187:1.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus carried his own cross, whereas The Urantia Book says only the crossbeam; Simon was a Cyrenian visitor going to the temple services, not coming in from the country, and later became a believer.
acts.note.187:2.desc: The soldiers bound Jesus' arms to the crossbeam and nailed his hands and feet. He tasted the drugged wine but refused it, and as they nailed him he prayed, "Father, forgive them." His mother, John, Ruth, and Jude arrived, and the soldiers divided his clothes and cast lots for the seamless robe.
acts.note.187:2.diff: The Bible speaks only of wine mixed with gall or myrrh, whereas The Urantia Book says a society of Jewish women offered drugged wine to lessen suffering; unlike John, it does not mention fulfilled prophecy.
acts.note.187:3.desc: About half past nine Jesus was hung on the cross, and more than a thousand people gathered. His mother, Mary Magdalene, and others stood nearby, while passers-by, Jewish rulers, and even the two thieves mocked him. After the crowd thinned, Jesus said, "I thirst," and the captain of the guard raised a sponge soaked in wine.
acts.note.187:3.diff: The Bible says the women watched from afar, whereas The Urantia Book says they stood near the cross; unlike Luke, the sour wine was not mockery but the captain's effort to relieve Jesus' thirst.
acts.note.187:4.desc: When one thief railed at Jesus, the other, who had often heard him teach, rebuked him and asked to be remembered when Jesus came into his kingdom. Jesus answered that he would sometime be with him in Paradise. This young man had admired Barabbas as a hero but found the true hero in Jesus.
acts.note.187:4.diff: Luke reads "today you will be with me in Paradise," whereas The Urantia Book reads "I say to you today, you shall sometime be" there; Luke heard the story from the converted Roman captain of the guard.
acts.note.sub:187:4.7.desc: About noon John returned with Jesus' mother and the women believers, and Jesus said to his mother, "Woman, behold your son!" and to John, "My son, behold your mother!" He then asked them to leave the place, and John and Jude led Mary away. She lived at John's home in Bethsaida and died less than a year later.
acts.note.sub:187:4.7.diff: The Gospel of John says only that the disciple took her into his home from that hour; The Urantia Book adds that Jesus asked them to leave, that Jude was present, and that Mary died in Bethsaida within a year.
acts.note.187:5.desc: After noon a sandstorm darkened the sky, and as his consciousness faded Jesus repeated portions of Psalms 20 to 22. Just before three o'clock he cried, "It is finished! Father, into your hands I commend my spirit," and died. The centurion came to believe in him, and a soldier pierced his side to make sure of his death.
acts.note.187:5.diff: The Bible presents the darkness, torn curtain, and earthquake as supernatural signs, whereas The Urantia Book explains the darkness as an Arabian sandstorm and omits the earthquake and opened tombs; the forsaken cry was a recited psalm.
acts.note.187:6.desc: About half past three David Zebedee sent out the last messengers with news of the Master's death to Bethany and elsewhere. John sent the women with Jude to the home of Elijah Mark and stayed at Golgotha until Joseph and Nicodemus came with Pilate's permission. The intelligences of the universe were shocked at the spectacle.
acts.note.188:0.desc: The Jewish rulers planned to throw Jesus' body into the open burial pits of Gehenna. Joseph of Arimathea, with Nicodemus, asked Pilate for the body, bringing a large sum of money in case a bribe was needed, but Pilate would not take money and quickly signed the order.
acts.note.188:0.diff: The Bible has Joseph go to Pilate alone, whereas The Urantia Book says Nicodemus accompanied him; instead of Mark's account of Pilate checking with the centurion, it says Pilate refused Joseph's money.
acts.note.188:1.desc: When representatives of the Sanhedrin tried to take the body, the centurion and his soldiers prevented them and gave it to Joseph. About half past four Joseph, Nicodemus, John, and the centurion carried it to Joseph's new rock tomb and wrapped it in bandages soaked in myrrh and aloes. The watching women resolved to return on Sunday morning.
acts.note.188:1.diff: The Bible says simply that Joseph or Nicodemus buried the body, whereas The Urantia Book says the Jews tried to seize it and that the centurion and John helped carry it; it also names more of the watching women.
acts.note.188:2.desc: About midnight on Friday the Jewish leaders met at Caiaphas's home, fearing Jesus' claim that he would rise on the third day. The next morning Pilate gave them ten soldiers, and they added ten temple guards to watch the tomb, rolled a second stone before it, and sealed it with Pilate's seal.
acts.note.188:2.diff: Matthew has Pilate say they have a guard and should go make the tomb secure, whereas The Urantia Book says Pilate gave ten Roman soldiers, who joined ten Jewish guards, making twenty in all.
acts.note.188:3.desc: Throughout the Sabbath the apostles stayed in hiding, gathering just before midnight on Saturday in the upper chamber of John Mark's home. The authors say they cannot fully explain the status of Jesus' personality during the thirty-six hours in the tomb, but think his human consciousness slept.
acts.note.188:4.desc: Jesus did not die to atone for mankind's guilt or to appease an offended God. Sin is not inherited; it is personal, deliberate rebellion, and ideas of ransom and atonement cannot be reconciled with God as a loving Father. Yet his death made the way of salvation clearer, so it is wholly correct to call him a savior.
acts.note.188:5.desc: The cross places all relations between God and man on the family basis of Father and son and reveals a love that lays down life even for enemies. The love of Jesus not only forgives sin but destroys it. The cross is not a sign of sacrifice to appease God's wrath but the symbol of unselfish service.
acts.note.189:0.desc: After Jesus' burial the chief of the archangels convened his council of the resurrection, but around midnight they concluded that creatures could not assist their Creator's return to life. Jesus' Personalized Adjuster told the celestial hosts that Michael had power to lay down his life and take it up again.
acts.note.189:1.desc: At two minutes past three o'clock on Sunday morning, April 9, A.D. 30, the resurrected morontia form and personality of Jesus came forth from Joseph's tomb. His physical body remained there in its linen wrappings, and the doorstones and Pilate's seals were undisturbed. He appeared as a morontia personality like the resurrected ascenders of the mansion worlds.
acts.note.189:2.desc: The chief of archangels asked Gabriel for Jesus' mortal body and received permission, and the celestial hosts dissolved it almost instantly. The secondary midwayers rolled away the stones from the tomb's entrance, and the frightened guards fled. The Jewish leaders bribed the twenty guards to say the disciples had stolen the body.
acts.note.189:2.diff: Matthew says an angel of the Lord descended amid an earthquake and rolled back the stone, whereas The Urantia Book credits the secondary midwayers; it explains the tomb was empty because the body was dissolved, not raised.
acts.note.189:3.desc: A little after half past four on Sunday morning, the morontia Michael directed Gabriel to begin the planetary resurrection roll call. The sleeping survivors of Urantia since the days of Adam then appeared in the resurrection halls of mansonia, the third dispensational resurrection.
acts.map37.head: Resurrection Day: Appearances in Jerusalem and Bethany
acts.map37.1.head: The tomb · to the five women
acts.map37.1.body: About half past three the five women from Joseph's house passed out of the Damascus gate and arrived before the empty tomb; Jesus, whom Mary Magdalene took for the caretaker of the garden, spoke to them. They hastened back to the Mark home (dashed).
acts.map37.2.head: The tomb · to Mary Magdalene
acts.map37.2.body: After Peter and John had seen the tomb and gone, he appeared again to Mary Magdalene, who lingered there.
acts.map37.3.head: Bethany · the garden of Lazarus
acts.map37.3.body: Shortly after noontide, to James, Jesus' oldest brother, standing in the garden of Lazarus before the empty tomb. Mary Magdalene had also come there.
acts.map37.4.head: Bethany · the home of Martha and Mary
acts.map37.4.body: Shortly before two o'clock, to his earthly family and their friends, twenty in all; he appeared in the open back door.
acts.map37.5.head: The home of Joseph of Arimathea
acts.map37.5.body: At about fifteen minutes past four, to some twenty-five women believers. Mary Magdalene had returned from Bethany a few minutes before (dashed).
acts.map37.6.head: The home of Flavius
acts.map37.6.body: About half past four, to some forty Greek believers, though the doors were securely fastened.
acts.map37.7.head: On the road to Emmaus
acts.map37.7.body: A few minutes before five, about three miles out of Jerusalem, to the brothers Cleopas and Jacob. Emmaus is about seven miles west of Jerusalem. They hastened back to Jerusalem (dashed).
acts.map37.8.head: The garden of the Mark home · to Peter
acts.map37.8.body: Near half past eight in the evening, to Simon Peter in the garden of the Mark home.
acts.map37.9.head: The upper chamber · to the ten apostles
acts.map37.9.body: Shortly after nine o'clock, in the midst of the ten apostles in the upper chamber with all the doors bolted. Thomas was not there.
acts.note.189:4.desc: About half past three on Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and four other women came to the tomb with ointments and found only the grave cloths. When a stranger they took for the caretaker of the garden called, "Mary," they recognized the Master. Jesus told them to tell the apostles, and Peter, that he had risen.
acts.note.189:4.diff: The Gospels have angels or a young man in white announce the resurrection at the tomb, whereas The Urantia Book has no angelic announcement; Jesus himself appeared to the women, whose names and number the Gospels vary but which it fixes at five.
acts.note.189:5.desc: Peter and John ran to the tomb and found it empty, with the grave cloths lying in order. Peter thought the body had been stolen, but John wondered why the cloths were left intact. After they left, Jesus appeared again to Mary Magdalene and had her tell the apostles he would go before them into Galilee.
acts.note.189:5.diff: The Gospel of John says the other disciple saw and believed, whereas The Urantia Book says neither apostle clearly understood what had happened, and Jesus then appeared to Mary a second time.
acts.note.190:0.desc: The resurrected Jesus remained briefly on Urantia to experience the morontia career that the mortals of Satania pass through on the mansion worlds. His morontia body had no circulating blood and did not take material food, yet it was real, so the believers who saw him were not deceived by hallucinations.
acts.note.190:1.desc: Hearing the women's report, Joseph and David Zebedee inspected the tomb, but at half past seven the captain of the temple guards removed the grave cloths. When the apostles doubted, David handed the money bag to Matthew and left; shortly before ten he sent his twenty-six messengers out with news of the resurrection and disbanded the messenger corps.
acts.note.190:2.desc: About noon on Sunday, in the garden of Lazarus at Bethany, Jesus made his third appearance, to his oldest brother James, calling him to the service of the kingdom. Shortly before two o'clock he appeared at the home of Martha and Mary to his earthly family and friends, twenty in all, bidding them enter the fellowship of the Spirit of Truth, and then vanished.
acts.note.190:3.desc: About a quarter past four on Sunday afternoon, Jesus made his fifth appearance, to some twenty-five women believers at the home of Joseph of Arimathea. He told them that in the kingdom there is neither Jew nor gentile, man nor woman, and sent them to publish the good news. As word spread, the Sanhedrin decided to expel from the synagogues anyone who spoke of the resurrection.
acts.note.190:4.desc: About half past four, though the doors were securely fastened, Jesus made his sixth appearance, to some forty Greek believers at the home of Flavius. He told them that in the Father's kingdom there would be neither Jew nor gentile, and charged them to proclaim the gospel of salvation to all the world. The Greeks remained together through the night.
acts.note.190:5.desc: A few minutes before five on Sunday afternoon, Jesus made his seventh appearance, to the shepherd brothers Cleopas and Jacob on the road to Emmaus, and explained the Scriptures to them. When he broke bread in their home, they recognized him, and he vanished. The brothers hurried back to Jerusalem and told the apostles in the upper chamber.
acts.note.190:5.diff: Luke names Cleopas and an unnamed disciple, whereas The Urantia Book identifies them as Cleopas and his unbelieving brother Jacob, shepherds of Emmaus; it lacks Luke's report that the Lord had appeared to Simon.
acts.note.191:0.desc: On resurrection Sunday ten apostles stayed in the upper chamber behind barred doors for fear of arrest, while Thomas brooded alone near Bethpage. John held firmly that Jesus had risen, and Peter wavered between faith and doubt. The Master delayed his first appearance so they could reflect on his words and so Thomas could be with them.
acts.note.191:1.desc: About half past eight on Sunday evening, Jesus made his eighth appearance, to Peter in the garden of the Mark home, telling him he had been forgiven even before asking and bidding him prepare to preach the gospel. When Peter declared he had seen the Master, Andrew hinted that Peter had seen things that were not real before.
acts.note.191:2.desc: Shortly after nine on Sunday evening, Jesus appeared in morontia form among the ten apostles in the upper chamber, though the doors were bolted. He rebuked their doubts, reminding them he had foretold his death and his rising on the third day, and told them to go to Galilee once all were together. This was his ninth appearance.
acts.note.191:2.diff: Luke and John say Jesus showed his hands, feet, and side and breathed on them to receive the Holy Spirit, whereas The Urantia Book has no such scene and instead tells them to go to Galilee when Thomas returns.
acts.note.191:3.desc: On Monday Jesus stayed with more than a million morontia directors and transition mortals from the seven mansion worlds. About midnight his form was adjusted to the second morontia stage, and he advanced stage by stage, attaining Jerusem citizenship on May 7. Thus Michael completed his seventh universe bestowal experience.
acts.map38.head: The Morontia Appearances, Tenth to Nineteenth
acts.map38.10.head: Philadelphia
acts.map38.10.body: A short time after eight o'clock on Tuesday, April 11, to Abner, Lazarus, and some one hundred and fifty of their associates in the synagogue.
acts.map38.11.head: Jerusalem · the Mark home
acts.map38.11.body: On Sunday evening, April 16, to the eleven apostles, Thomas now with them. Very early the next morning the apostles started out for Galilee.
acts.map38.12.head: Alexandria (overview)
acts.map38.12.body: On Tuesday evening, April 18, at about half past eight, to Rodan and some eighty other believers.
acts.map38.13.head: The shore at Bethsaida
acts.map38.13.body: About six o'clock on Friday, April 21, to the ten apostles as their boat drew near the shore after a night of fishing. The first appearance in Galilee.
acts.map38.14.head: The hill near Capernaum
acts.map38.14.body: At noon on Saturday, April 22, to the eleven apostles on the very mount where he had set them apart as apostles.
acts.map38.15.head: Bethsaida
acts.map38.15.body: On Saturday, April 29, at three o'clock, to more than five hundred believers assembled to hear Peter preach.
acts.map38.16.head: Jerusalem · the courtyard of Nicodemus
acts.map38.16.body: On Friday, May 5, about nine o'clock at night, to the eleven apostles, the women's corps, and about fifty other leading disciples.
acts.map38.17.head: Near Jacob's well, at Sychar
acts.map38.17.body: About four o'clock on Sabbath afternoon, May 13, to Nalda and about seventy-five Samaritan believers.
acts.map38.18.head: Tyre
acts.map38.18.body: On Tuesday, May 16, a little before nine o'clock in the evening, to believers about to disperse.
acts.map38.19.head: Jerusalem · last appearance and farewell
acts.map38.19.body: Early Thursday morning, May 18, to the eleven apostles in the upper chamber of Mary Mark's home; at almost half past seven, on the western slope of Mount Olivet, he took leave and vanished from their sight.
acts.note.191:4.desc: A little after eight o'clock on Tuesday, April 11, Jesus made his tenth appearance, to Abner, Lazarus, and about one hundred fifty believers in the synagogue at Philadelphia. He told them to love and serve all men as he had loved them and to fellowship all gospel workers. The next morning they went out proclaiming the resurrection.
acts.note.191:5.desc: Thomas returned on Saturday, April 15, but would not believe. The next evening, as he said he must put his finger in the nail marks, Jesus appeared and said, "As the Father sent me into the world, so send I you." Thomas fell to his knees, crying, "I believe!" and before dawn the apostles set out for Galilee.
acts.note.191:5.diff: The Gospel of John has Jesus invite Thomas to touch the nail marks and his side, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus was raised in morontia form and had no nail marks on his hands.
acts.note.191:6.desc: About half past eight on Tuesday evening, April 18, Jesus made his twelfth appearance, to Rodan and some eighty believers in Alexandria, just as Nathan, David's messenger, finished reporting the crucifixion. Jesus told them the gospel belongs to all men and that the Spirit of Truth would soon come.
acts.note.192:0.desc: With the apostles in hiding, the Jewish leaders quieted down, believing the movement suppressed. From this time Peter was by common consent the head of the apostolic corps, and Matthias, later chosen in Judas's place, became treasurer. Early Monday the apostles left for Galilee with John Mark, reaching Bethsaida late on Wednesday night.
acts.note.192:1.desc: On Friday morning, April 21, after a fruitless night of fishing, ten apostles were told by a man on the beach to cast the net on the right side, and it filled. When John recognized the Master, Peter leaped into the water. They counted 153 large fish, and Jesus ate breakfast with them and talked for more than an hour.
acts.note.192:1.diff: The Gospel of John presents this as a miracle, whereas The Urantia Book calls it only the Master's preknowledge of where the fish were; John Mark dressed the fish, and Simon Zelotes was absent, having gone home.
acts.note.192:2.desc: After breakfast Jesus walked the beach with the apostles two by two. He told John to love men, and three times asked Peter if he loved him, bidding him feed his sheep. With the other pairs he spoke of trust, service, obedience, and belief, then said he would meet them the next day on the mount of their ordination.
acts.note.192:2.diff: The Gospel of John reports only the exchange with Peter and a prediction of his death, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus talked with all the apostles in pairs and contains no prediction of Peter's death.
acts.note.192:3.desc: At noon on Saturday, April 22, Jesus made his fourteenth appearance, to the eleven apostles on the hill near Capernaum where he had ordained them. Kneeling in a circle about him, they heard him repeat their charges and re-enact the ordination, and he prayed with words of power. No one then saw him for a full week.
acts.note.192:3.diff: Matthew records a command on the mountain to make disciples of all nations, baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whereas The Urantia Book reports only the re-enacted ordination and prayer, with no such command.
acts.note.192:4.desc: At three o'clock on Saturday, April 29, more than five hundred believers at Bethsaida heard Peter's first public sermon since the resurrection, and as he finished, Jesus made his fifteenth appearance. Back in Jerusalem, the apostles in the upper chamber began proclaiming the resurrection in place of the gospel of the kingdom.
acts.note.193:0.desc: About nine o'clock on Friday night, May 5, Jesus made his sixteenth appearance, in the courtyard of Nicodemus, to the eleven, the women's corps, and some fifty disciples. He said his resurrection did not change his message; sonship with God by faith remains the saving truth. He told them to tarry in Jerusalem.
acts.note.193:1.desc: About four o'clock on Sabbath afternoon, May 13, Jesus made his seventeenth appearance, to Nalda and about seventy-five Samaritan believers near Jacob's well at Sychar. He taught that salvation is God's free gift received by faith but must be followed by the fruits of the spirit life, and told them to love and serve their brethren with family affection.
acts.note.193:2.desc: On Tuesday evening, May 16, as a meeting of believers at Tyre was breaking up, Jesus made his eighteenth appearance. He taught that the rising of the dead is not the gospel itself, and that those born of the spirit must bear its fruits, such as loving service. The news spread to Sidon and even Antioch.
acts.note.193:3.desc: Early Thursday morning, May 18, Jesus appeared for the last time to the eleven in the upper chamber and told them to tarry in Jerusalem until they received the Spirit of Truth. When Simon Zelotes asked about restoring the kingdom, he corrected the idea of a material kingdom and, citing Judas as an example, urged them to trust one another.
acts.note.193:3.diff: Luke has Jesus open the Scriptures about Christ's suffering and the preaching of repentance for forgiveness, whereas The Urantia Book records his answer to Simon Zelotes and his plea for mutual trust, citing Judas's isolation.
acts.note.193:4.desc: In light of the Master's farewell, the narrator reviews why Judas fell. He was an isolated personality who would not confide in his fellows, he failed to grow in love and grace, and he blamed others for disappointments while nursing grudges. Thomas and Nathaniel, who had similar tendencies, learned to trust their brethren more.
acts.note.193:5.desc: Almost half past seven on Thursday morning, May 18, Jesus reached the western slope of Mount Olivet with the eleven. He bade them preach the gospel to the uttermost parts of the world when the Spirit of Truth came, and to love and serve men; about seven forty-five he vanished and returned by way of Jerusem and Edentia to Salvington.
acts.note.193:5.diff: Luke says he was carried up to heaven while blessing them near Bethany, whereas The Urantia Book says that on Olivet's western slope he simply vanished from sight, as he had many times during the forty days.
acts.note.193:6.desc: At Peter's direction, by ten thirty one hundred and twenty disciples, including Jesus' mother Mary and his brother James, gathered at the Mark home, and Peter reported the farewell and ascension. Downstairs the eleven cast lots, and Matthias was chosen in Judas's place. Later Nathaniel and others withdrew, leaving six apostles in the Jerusalem proclamation.
acts.note.193:6.diff: Acts says Peter cited the Psalms about Judas's end and all prayed before casting lots, whereas The Urantia Book says the eleven went downstairs and cast lots by themselves.
acts.intro.194: The Spirit of Truth poured out
acts.note.194:0.desc: About one o'clock on the day of the ascension, as the one hundred and twenty prayed at the Mark home, they became aware of a strange presence in the room and felt spiritual joy and confidence. Peter declared this must be the promised Spirit of Truth and proposed going to the temple. But they fell into preaching the risen Lord instead of the fatherhood and sonship.
acts.note.194:0.diff: Acts describes a rushing mighty wind, tongues as of fire, and speaking in other languages, whereas The Urantia Book says those quietly praying merely sensed a presence in the room and an inner joy.
acts.note.194:1.desc: About two o'clock on Pentecost, Peter made an impassioned appeal in the very place where the Master had last taught in the temple. Six apostles preached the risen Messiah for more than an hour and a half in Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic, and by half past four more than two thousand new believers were baptized at the pool of Siloam.
acts.note.194:1.diff: Acts tells of hearers each understanding in their own tongue and three thousand converts, whereas The Urantia Book says the apostles spoke languages they knew and that more than two thousand were baptized at Siloam.
acts.note.194:2.desc: The Spirit of Truth, sent in Jesus' place, restates his message for each new generation, keeps believers from feeling orphaned, and makes them conscious not of himself but of Michael. Since its bestowal, man has received a threefold spirit endowment: the Thought Adjuster, the Spirit of Truth, and the Holy Spirit.
acts.note.194:3.desc: The Spirit of Truth teaches the Father's love and the Son's mercy and reveals the Creator Son within the heart. Pentecost freed the religion of Jesus from national and racial fetters, from rituals and sacred places, and from physical force, and women stood equal with men. The spirit was given to all sincere believers.
acts.note.194:4.desc: After Pentecost the apostles preached the risen Christ and his return instead of the gospel of the kingdom. The early believers shared their goods, baptized in the name of Jesus, and through Gamaliel's counsel enjoyed a season of peace. But after Stephen's death persecution broke out, scattering believers throughout the empire.
acts.note.sub:194:4.12.desc: Stephen, leader of the Greek believers in Jerusalem, became the first martyr to the new faith. The believers then realized they could no longer go on as a sect within Judaism, and within a month the church at Jerusalem was organized under Peter's leadership, with James the brother of Jesus as its titular head.
acts.note.sub:194:4.12.diff: Acts tells of Stephen's vision of the opened heavens and the Son of Man and introduces Saul, whereas The Urantia Book says he was stoned without trial during a sermon, which directly led to the church's organization.
acts.note.195:0.desc: After Pentecost Peter became the real founder of the Christian church, Paul carried its message to the gentiles, and Greek believers spread it through the Roman Empire. Christianity triumphed over rival religions through organization, Hellenization, and compromises with Mithraism and paganism.
acts.note.195:1.desc: The Hellenization of Christianity began in earnest when Paul spoke to the Areopagus in Athens about the Unknown God. Greek intellectual freedom joined with the spiritual liberty of Jesus to form a charter of human freedom. Greeks seeking one God embraced Christianity.
acts.note.195:2.desc: Rome brought the West tolerance of other languages, peoples, and religions; early persecution arose because the word "kingdom" was misunderstood as political rivalry. Honest, self-governing Romans accepted Christianity as a moral philosophy, and Stoicism and Greek belief in immortality also helped prepare its acceptance.
acts.note.195:3.desc: Rome provided political unity, Greece cultural unity, and Christianity religious unity. What gave Christianity its greatest power was the way believers lived lives of service and even died for their faith under persecution. Yet Christianity could not stop Rome's moral decline or the empire's collapse.
acts.note.195:4.desc: In Europe's dark ages the church, bound to society and politics, shared their decline, and religion became monastic, ascetic, and legalized. The individual was nearly lost before church authority and tradition, and the idea of seeking the intercession of saints arose. Still, Christianity survived with its moral influence and revived in many sects after the Renaissance.
acts.note.195:5.desc: To solve the problems of the twentieth century, men must first seek the realities of heaven. Religion is a personal, spiritual experience, distinct from logic, aesthetic appreciation, ethics, and even moral sense, and it culminates in worship. Jesus followed the method of experience, and love is the guide to true insight.
acts.note.195:6.desc: Scientists have unintentionally thrown mankind into a materialistic panic, but the religion of Jesus has never gone bankrupt. Science is a quantitative experience and religion a qualitative one, so true religion cannot quarrel with science. Concepts of truth, beauty, and goodness are not inherent in physics or chemistry, and a machine cannot know truth.
acts.note.195:7.desc: If the universe were only material and man only a machine, man could never recognize himself as a machine. The very mind of the scientist who builds a mechanistic philosophy proves itself supermaterial. The scientist, not science, the artist, not art, and the religionist, not religion, demonstrate respectively the universe, the morontia world, and spirit reality.
acts.note.195:8.desc: Modern secularism was born of godless science as father and the totalitarian medieval church as mother. Secularism broke the church's fetters but delivers man into bondage to the totalitarian state, and the brotherhood of men cannot be built while ignoring God. The wars of the first third of the twentieth century are only the beginning of that harvest.
acts.note.195:9.desc: Paganized and socialized Christianity needs new contact with the uncompromised teachings of Jesus, and religion needs new spiritual leaders who will depend solely on Jesus and his teachings. Modern men fear that the religion of Jesus might dominate and transform them, and most people experience religion secondhand through their teachers.
acts.note.195:10.desc: What the world now most needs is Jesus, seen living again in the experience of spirit-born mortals. The true church, the brotherhood of Jesus, is invisible and spiritual. The hope of Christianity lies in learning anew the gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of men.
acts.note.196:0.desc: Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God, a personal and spiritual faith born of the indwelling Adjuster. His faith had a child's trust but was neither childish nor fanatical. He did not ask his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him.
acts.note.196:1.desc: However great the sovereignty of Michael, the human Jesus must not be taken from men; he was the truest religionist who ever lived on Urantia. To follow Jesus is not to imitate his outward life but to share his faith. He ascended from the human to the divine through seven stages.
acts.note.196:2.desc: The gospel of the kingdom rests on the religious experience of Jesus of Galilee, whereas Christianity rests almost wholly on Paul's experience. Jesus founded a religion of doing God's will and serving the brotherhood; Paul founded one of worshiping the glorified Christ. Jesus saw most men as weak rather than wicked, yet all were God's children.
acts.note.196:3.desc: Personal, spiritual religious experience is an efficient solvent for most mortal difficulties. The evidences of the indwelling Adjuster are love, wisdom, and worship. The Hebrews had a religion of moral sublimity and the Greeks a religion of beauty, but Jesus revealed and exemplified a religion of love.
